body.text: Spot prices of crude oil and yields on French government bonds jumped on September 10. On that day, Yemen-based Houthis—an AI-literate militia with an extraordinary range of modern weapons—seized control of Bab-el-Mandab, the Red Sea’s southern chokepoint, even as Iran’s Iraqi allies bombed Saudi Arabia’s vital East-West pipeline. With Iran already restricting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the primary alternative corridor for Gulf oil was severely downgraded.

Since then, despite brief pullbacks, spot oil prices and French yields have marched upward. Why does a geopolitical shock in West Asia translate into a crisis for French credibility? Are other countries at similar risk? Should India worry?

Sovereign bond yields have been rising across the developed world since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. The primary upward pressure on yields is due toincreasing government debt-to-GDP ratios and aggressive borrowing by tech firms financing gargantuan AI data centres. But critical moments in the war have heightened panic. Bond investors, fearing that surging energy costs will ignite runaway inflation and erode the future value of their earnings, are demanding steadily increasing interest rates.

The Houthi attack was a marker that West Asia’s conflict has no evident end. An unbottled genie is marauding as the “spot” price of crude oil—the price paid for immediate possession. While spot prices and commonly cited futures contracts typically track in lockstep, Trump administration insiders have broken that link. They have aggressively bid down futures prices to sell a political narrative that the war is causing little economic damage and will soon end. The paper-based futures prices have become irrelevant. Since September 10, the spot price for physical crude has gained an astronomical $20 to $25 premium over futures; traders who deal with barrels, not paper, are howling.

This premium reflects an upheaval in global energy logistics. The maritime tracking firm Kpler believes that Gulf states are likely paying Iran a protection fee of 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the cargo's total value to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Ships attempting to evade this fee risk Iranian missile attacks. In addition, according to The New York Times, shipping and insurance premiums are tacking $34 per barrel onto the final delivery cost.

Even not counting the additional shipping and insurance costs, spot prices of crude oil in the range of $120 to $130 per barrel are over 70 per cent above pre-war levels; global LNG prices have more than doubled since the war’s start. This exposes France’s vulnerability: despite its domestic nuclear capacity, a near-total dependence on imported oil and gas threatens to balloon its massive 5.4 per cent budget deficit as the government appeases domestic constituents.

France was a socio-economic tinderbox; the West Asian escalation provided the match. France’s on-edge public and dysfunctional domestic politics have collided with its historical tendency to run fiscal deficits, exacerbated by its membership in a currency union that encourages fiscal indiscipline.

Since 2019, France’s debt-to-GDP ratio has galloped by 20 percentage points to a staggering 118 per cent. Now, by punishing France with higher bond yields, investors may be on the verge of locking the nation into a vicious debt trap wherein rising yields push up deficits and debts, inviting further increase in yields.

Following the September 10 energy shock, public anger boiled over on September 15 as unions protested over poor pay and rising fuel prices, and workers disrupted the Dunkirk LNG terminal. French fishermen followed by blocking Mediterranean ports over rising fuel costs. This unrest quickly fused with a student revolt over crumbling, underfunded high schools, drawing 2,50,000 demonstrators onto the streets of Paris, Marseille, and Lyon. Stranded between a cost-of-living crisis and financial market panic, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised to release 10 million barrels of strategic diesel reserves in early October to suppress pump prices and quell spreading instability.

But Lecornu’s Band-Aids cannot heal the country’s broken politics. The fractured National Assembly lacks a ruling majority and the political appetite to pass a disciplined budget that raises taxes and reins in spending. Compounding the problem, the candidates angling to replace President Emmanuel Macron in seven months are campaigning on platforms that would blow up the budget entirely.

While domestic dysfunction bears the immediate blame, the architecture of the Eurozone provided the permissive structure for this fiscal rot. As I argued in EuroTragedy (Oxford University Press) in 2018, the euro was a jugaad—a makeshift, ill-fitting compromise—of mismatched political ideas and incentives. Its architects ducked the threat of sovereign overspending. They forbade by treaty the bailing out of spendthrift member states and established quaint statutory limits—capping annual deficits at 3 per cent of the GDP and total debt at 60 per cent—only to watch Italy violate them instantly. Instead of falling, Italian debt-to-GDP ratios rose. Other Eurozone countries followed quickly.

Such fiscal irresponsibility seemed costless until July 2012, when the out-of-control sovereign debt crisis triggered an existential crisis. With Italy and Spain on the brink of default, European Central Bank (ECB) President Mario Draghi famously declared that the central bank would do “whatever it takes” to save the euro. While the promise was celebrated as a master stroke of central banking, markets believed that Draghi had pledged to print unlimited money to repay the debts of member states. Unlike the US monetary union—where States and bond investors know that no federal bailout is coming—the Eurozone permanently erased market discipline.

Amid COVID-19-era stresses, an unaccountable ECB—waving away its treaty-based restriction—reinforced Draghi’s pledge. It began purchasing sovereign debt to bid down yields before a bailout became necessary. In effect, the ECB began funding heavily indebted countries at below-market interest rates. France started outpacing Italy as the poster child of this fiscal dependency. Bond markets are now daring the ECB to continue funding France.

While the ECB has the raw monetary power to stare down markets, European politics are fraying. Germany’s political establishment is distinctly unamused: Germany is effectively underwriting its neighbours’ mounting debts through the ECB’s internal accounting mechanisms. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party—born as an anti-euro party in 2013, soon after Draghi’s bailout promise—has gained rapid electoral traction, reviving its opposition to the euro (alongside its anti-immigration stance and Nazi proclivities). Germany and other “creditor” countries are also moving to slash the European Union’s budget. The ultimate political jugaad, the euro faces a political reckoning.

These tremors have not yet triggered a global financial earthquake, but the geopolitical tectonic plates are shifting rapidly. The West Asia conflict is expanding daily. On October 10, a Houthi attack killed 13 people and injured hundreds of others at a Riyadh airport, forcing its temporary closure. Another attack extensively damaged the headquarters of the oil company Aramco. The Iranians have escalated attacks on ships trying to bypass their surveillance in the Strait of Hormuz, sinking one large oil carrier. The unbottled energy genie is also threatening critical undersea communication cables beneath the Bab-el-Mandab, multiplying systemic damage.

As other dominoes fall, India eerily mirrors France. India’s combined fiscal deficit of 7.5 per cent of GDP (as per the IMF) is locked in rigid budgetary entitlements, added to which opaque public accounts mask the true cost of shielding consumers from soaring energy prices. Fleeing foreign portfolio investors are shattering India’s credibility—just as bond markets are undermining France—dragging India’s stock and currency markets to the worst-performing among major economies. With the youth equally anxious and furious about education and its future, India is piling dry wood—waiting for a global match to strike.
Ashoka Mody retired from Princeton University. He previously worked for the World Bank and the IMF. He is the author of India is Broken: A People Betrayed, Independence to Today (2023).
